Save as many dates and trips as you like, plan them together on both your phones, get a reminder the day before each one and open a whole date in Apple or Google Maps; and while it runs, every gift template and every game pack is yours. One of you pays, monthly or yearly; the other joins with the invite link you send.

A year of everything for the two of you: as many saved dates and trips as you like, planned together on both your phones, a reminder the day before each one, a whole date opened in Apple or Google Maps, and every gift template and game pack. One of you pays once; the other joins with the invite link you send. It lasts 365 days and doesn't renew by itself.

Ethos for Two is: one payment a month or a year covers both of you, and it renews until you cancel, which you can do at any time from your account page. Everything else here is paid once: templates, “Make it special” and game packs stay on your account for good.

No. Ethos for Two is one payment for 365 days, for both of you, and it doesn't renew by itself: we email you two weeks before it ends, and renewing is one tap. Templates, “Make it special” and game packs are one-time payments too, and stay on your account for good.

faq.q: Can my partner use it on their phone?
faq.a: Yes, that's the point of it. After paying you get an invite link: your partner opens it on their phone and signs in (free), and from then on you both see and edit the same saved dates, and every template and pack is on their account too. One partner only; you can remove them, or they can leave, at any time.

From your account page: Cancel membership, then confirm. It's as quick as subscribing. Nothing more is charged, and you both keep Ethos for Two until the end of the month or year you've paid for. Your saved dates stay in your account, and gifts you've published stay online.

faq.q: Can we switch between monthly and yearly?
faq.a: Yes, from your account page. Monthly to yearly happens at once: you pay for the year, minus what's left of your month. Yearly to monthly happens when your year ends, so you never pay twice.

faq.q: What happens to our saved dates if we stop?
faq.a: Nothing is deleted. Your saved dates and trips stay in your account and stay yours; you just stop sharing them. The free plan keeps your three most recently changed ones editable and the rest readable, until you delete some or come back. Gifts you've published stay online.

faq.q: Can I change my mind after subscribing?
faq.a: Yes. You can withdraw within 14 days of subscribing, without giving a reason: use “Withdraw from a purchase” at the foot of every page, or reply to your welcome email. Because you asked for it to start straight away, we refund what you paid minus the days you've already used. After 14 days you can still cancel at any time; it then runs to the end of the period you've paid for.

faq.q: Can I change my mind after buying?
faq.a: Yes, within 14 days of buying, without giving a reason: use “Withdraw from a purchase” at the foot of every page, or reply to your receipt. Because you asked for your year to start straight away, we refund what you paid minus the days you've already used.

faq.q: What does the free tier actually include?
faq.a: Finding a date, planning it and sending it as a link, with the forecast and the sunset; the long-distance tools; and the games. No account needed, and a free account keeps up to three saved dates or trips. For gifts: two full templates (The Letter and Constellations), unlimited gifts, up to 10 photos per gift, our music library, a 30-second preview of a real song they can tap to hear, a countdown and a hidden final surprise, with a small “Made with Ethos” footer. Video clips, voice messages, up to 20 photos, a surprise inside, no footer, scheduling and a password come with “Make it special”, with any unlock, or with Ethos for Two.

faq.q: Can I try a template before paying?
faq.a: Every template has a full live demo, and the editor is free to use with a live preview. You only pay when you publish something that needs a premium feature.

Buy “Give Everything” and we email you a code (it's on the confirmation page too). Pass it on however you like: whoever redeems it gets every template, forever, on their own account. A code can be redeemed for two years.
Extra decks for the games: more questions, bolder dares. Each one is a one-time payment and yours for good, and every pack comes with Ethos for Two while it runs. The games themselves stay free.
Yes. Whoever receives a gift you paid for can send you one back in the same template, free, with the small “Made with Ethos” footer. If they want extras or no footer on it, they pay the normal price.
No. The price on this page is the price for everyone, and we don't run discount codes. Creators who share Ethos are paid a commission by us through their own link; it never changes what you pay.
No. Links are meant to be permanent. If we ever had to change that we'd give you at least 90 days' notice.

faq.q: Can I edit a gift after it's live?
faq.a: Yes. Edits go live at the same link the moment you save.
Prices are in euros, VAT included where it applies, and Stripe Checkout shows the final amount in your currency before you pay. Card, Apple Pay, Google Pay and other methods, through Stripe.

Templates, “Make it special” and game packs: at checkout you ask us to unlock your purchase straight away and tick that you then lose the 14-day right to cancel. If a gift won't open or play properly on their phone and we can't fix it, tell us within 30 days and you get your money back. Ethos for Two is different: it's a service, so you can withdraw within 14 days and we refund what you paid, less the days you've used. Gift cards: change your mind within 14 days, before the code is redeemed, and we refund you in full. “Withdraw from a purchase”, at the foot of every page, says how.

notes.london: Most of London's big museums are free, so the museum date costs only the glass of something after. And with the West End so close, a night at the theater is an easy yes.
notes.manchester: The center is compact, so dinner, a film and a late dessert rarely need more than a walk between them.
notes.edinburgh: Calton Hill is a short walk from Princes Street and costs nothing, which makes getting up for the sunrise an easy sell.
notes.dublin: The National Gallery and the National Museum are free to walk into, which is exactly what a wet afternoon needs.
notes.birmingham: The canals run right through the center, with towpaths and waterside tables at Brindleyplace and Gas Street Basin: the long way home is along the water.
notes.glasgow: The big museums are free here, Kelvingrove and the Gallery of Modern Art among them, so a wet afternoon costs nothing but the coffee after.
notes.bristol: Brandon Hill is a short climb from the harbor, and Cabot Tower at the top is free to go up. It is the place for the golden hour.
notes.leeds: The Victorian arcades in the center keep you under glass between dinner and dessert. The Hyde Park Picture House, open since 1914, is still lit by gas lamps.
notes.liverpool: There is live music on Mathew Street, round the Cavern Club, most nights. Before it, the national museums by the waterfront are free for the afternoon.
notes.new-york: Pick two stops in the same neighborhood and walk between them: in New York, the streets are half the date.
notes.los-angeles: Distances are long here, so choose one neighborhood and keep the date in it. The beach at sunset is worth the drive.
notes.chicago: The lakefront has sandy beaches a short ride from the Loop, so the beach date is closer than you'd think.
notes.san-francisco: Most neighborhoods have a hilltop park within a steep walk, and they are the best seats in town for the golden hour.
notes.miami: Midday heat is serious for much of the year, so the ideas for early mornings and evenings come first.
notes.boston: The center is small and walkable, and the Public Garden, with its lagoon, sits right in the middle of it.
notes.dallas: The Dallas Museum of Art is free to walk into, and Klyde Warren Park, built on a deck over the freeway, is across the street for the walk after.
notes.kansas-city: Barbecue is the dinner here, and it suits the twist: order for each other, no vetoes. On the first Friday of the month the Crossroads galleries stay open late.
notes.houston: The Museum District has nineteen museums around Hermann Park, and some never charge, the Menil Collection and the Contemporary Arts Museum among them. Go late in the day, when the heat lets up.
notes.atlanta: The BeltLine's Eastside Trail follows an old railway from Piedmont Park to Krog Street, past patios and places to stop. It is a walk made for an ice cream.
notes.austin: From spring to fall, over a million bats fly out from under the Congress Avenue Bridge at dusk, so a golden hour by Lady Bird Lake ends with a show.
notes.denver: City Park's lake has the view the city is known for: the skyline with the Rockies behind it. Bring the picnic an hour before sunset, and a jacket, even in summer.
notes.milwaukee: The art museum on the lakefront has wings: a sunshade that opens when the museum does and folds at closing, if the wind allows. See it, then find a beer nearby.
notes.salt-lake-city: Ensign Peak is a short, steep walk above the Capitol: about twenty minutes up, and at sunset the whole valley and the lake are below you.
notes.san-antonio: The River Walk runs a level below the streets, shaded by cypress trees, so the long way home after dinner is cooler than the street above.
notes.columbus: On the first Saturday of the month the Short North holds its Gallery Hop: the galleries along High Street stay open late and the street fills up.
notes.orlando: Lake Eola sits in the middle of downtown, with swan-shaped pedal boats to rent and a path around the water that takes about twenty minutes.
notes.philadelphia: Many of the city's small restaurants are BYOB: you bring the bottle, they bring the glasses. Dinner for two starts at the wine shop.
notes.phoenix: In the hot months the city gets up early: the trails are busy at sunrise and quiet by mid-morning. Do the same, and keep the afternoon for somewhere with air conditioning.
notes.pittsburgh: The Duquesne Incline, a cable railway from 1877, climbs Mount Washington for a few dollars. The view from the top is where the three rivers meet.
notes.portland: Powell's fills a whole city block with books, new and used on the same shelves, which makes “pick a book for each other” a long and happy job.
notes.seattle: It drizzles more often than it pours here, which is what the city's coffee shops and big independent bookshops are for. On a clear evening, Kerry Park has the skyline.
notes.st-louis: Forest Park holds the art museum, the history museum and the zoo, and all three are free. In winter its outdoor rink opens for skating.
notes.nashville: The honky-tonks on Lower Broadway have live bands from late morning to closing time and rarely charge at the door. The bands play for tips, so bring a few dollars in cash.
notes.san-diego: Balboa Park puts gardens and more than a dozen museums in one place, and the beaches are a short ride from it. Start in the park and finish at the sunset.
notes.toronto: The islands are a short ferry ride from downtown, with beaches, paths and a view of the skyline back.
notes.vancouver: Stanley Park and the seawall start at the edge of downtown, so an outdoor date needs no car.
notes.montreal: Winters are long and cold, so ice rinks and hot chocolate aren't a novelty here: they're the season. For the view, walk up Mount Royal.
notes.sydney: The beaches, the harbor and its ferries are all part of the city, so the ideas by the water come first.
notes.melbourne: Laneways, galleries and kitchens that stay open late: this is a city for an evening that runs longer than planned.
notes.auckland: The weather can change in an afternoon here, so keep an indoor idea in your pocket for when it turns.
notes.paris: A picnic by the river is a local habit, and some of the big museums stay open late one evening a week.
notes.amsterdam: It rains a fair bit, and the city is full of small galleries and big museums for exactly those days.
notes.berlin: Late nights are normal here, so the evening ideas can start later than you'd plan anywhere else.
notes.munich: The English Garden, one of the largest city parks anywhere, is a short walk from the center.
notes.vienna: The coffee houses are made for staying: nobody will hurry you away from a table for two.
notes.prague: The old center is at its quietest early in the morning, which is when the bridges belong to the two of you.
notes.copenhagen: Renting a small boat for the canals and the harbor is a summer habit here, and nobody expects you to know how to sail.
notes.stockholm: The city is built on islands, so walking between two stops usually means walking along the water.
notes.oslo: The fjord starts at the edge of the center, and the opera house roof is free to walk up for the view.
notes.lisbon: The miradouros, the city's lookout terraces, are free and made for the golden hour.
notes.rome: Gelato and a slow walk through the center: a date the city has had a long time to perfect.
notes.riga: The Old Town is small enough to cross in a quarter of an hour, and the canal parks run right alongside it.
notes.tallinn: The Old Town has viewing platforms over its rooftops, a short climb from the main square.
notes.singapore: The heat is steady and afternoon downpours are common, so indoor and evening ideas sit near the top: eat late, then walk once the air cools.
notes.dubai: For much of the year it's too hot to be out at midday, so evenings and indoor ideas come first, an ice rink included. For the stars, head to the desert.

paidMissing.label: I paid but can't find my gift
paidMissing.answer: A gift is saved on the phone or computer it was made on until it's published. Sign in with the email you paid with, on that same phone or computer, and open My gifts: at the top it says your gift is paid for. Tap “Finish and send it”. On a different phone the draft isn't there, so make the gift again in the same template: it's already unlocked, so there's nothing more to pay.

signIn.label: I can't sign in
signIn.answer: There are no passwords: type your email on the sign-in page and we send you a link and a 6-digit code. Each link works once, for an hour, and a newer email replaces an older one, so use the newest, or type its 6-digit code. Nothing after a few minutes? Check spam and promotions. Sign in with the email you paid with, or your purchases won't be there.

prices.label: Prices and paying
prices.answer: Templates are paid once and nothing renews: one template {single}, any three {pick3}, every template {everything}, and “Make it special” on a free template {extras}. {forTwo} The Letter is free as a short note; its photos and full letter come with “Make it special”. You pay on Stripe's page with a card, Apple Pay or Google Pay, and there are no discount codes.
prices.forTwoPass: Ethos for Two is {pass} for a year for both of you, paid once, and it doesn't renew by itself.
prices.forTwoSubscription: Ethos for Two is {monthly} a month or {yearly} a year for both of you, renewing until you cancel it on your Account page.

edit.label: Changing or resending a gift
edit.answer: Open My gifts and tap “Edit” on the gift: your changes go live at the same link as soon as you publish them, so there's nothing to resend. “Copy link” gives you the link again, and “QR card” a card to print.

wontOpen.label: The gift won't open
wontOpen.answer: Gift links open in any phone or computer browser, with no app and no account. If it says it isn't open yet, it's scheduled for a set time; if it asks for a password, it's the one the sender chose. If the words show in another language, the browser is translating the page: turn translation off for that page.

refunds.label: Refunds
refunds.answer: Templates, “Make it special” and game packs are unlocked straight away at checkout, which ends the 14-day right to cancel. If a gift won't open or play properly and we can't fix it, tell us within 30 days of buying and you get your money back. Ethos for Two can be withdrawn within 14 days, refunded minus the days used. Our team decides every refund.
